questions.q:
Kabir in Bhopal grows a tomato sapling in a pot on a covered balcony where direct sunlight never reaches; his mother waters it daily. His grandfather says, 'Water it twice a day and it will catch up with the neighbour's sapling on the open terrace.' Kabir's family will be away for two weeks. Plan P: leave the pot on the balcony, where an aunt will water it every day. Plan Q: carry it to the sunny terrace, where nobody can water it during the two weeks.
(a) Which pot of Activity 10.1 is the balcony sapling like, and which is the terrace sapling under plan Q like?
(b) Evaluate the grandfather's advice.
(c) What does the book lead you to expect for each plan after the two weeks?
(d) Which plan should Kabir choose for these two weeks, and why?
questions.a: (a) The balcony sapling is like pot C (water, no sunlight); the terrace sapling under plan Q is like pot B (sunlight, no water). (b) Extra water cannot replace sunlight: pot C is watered every day and still grows less than pot A. (c) Plan P: the plant grows less than a sunlit, watered plant. Plan Q: the plant may die, as the pot B plant may. (d) Plan P, because the book says the pot B plant may die while the pot C plant only grows less; he can move it into the sun once someone can water it daily.
s: Part (a): balcony = pot C, plan Q terrace = pot B
Part (b): extra water cannot replace sunlight, citing pot C
Part (c): P grows less, Q may die
Part (d): chooses P, because dying is worse than slower growth, and plans a later move

questions.q:
Chandni's version of Table 10.1 has columns for height, number of leaves and colour of leaves only. The book says that as a plant grows, new leaves and branches emerge, its height increases and its stem thickens.
(a) Name a change of growth that the book lists but her table has no column for.
(b) Suggest one way she could record it for pots A, B and C.
questions.a: (a) New branches emerging, or the thickening of the stem (either is accepted). (b) For branches, count the branches on each plant on Day 1 and after two weeks; for the stem, measure its thickness on both days. Her table then shows change as it does for height.
s: Part (a): branches emerging or stem thickening
Part (b): a way to record it on Day 1 and after two weeks

questions.q: Priya says: 'Pots A and C are both watered every day, so the fact that pot A's sapling grows better shows that the missing sunlight made pot C's sapling grow less.' Do you agree? Explain with Activity 10.1.
questions.a: Yes. Pots A and C differ only in sunlight (A is in direct sunlight, C is in the dark) and both get water. The book says A grows better than C, so the difference can be put down to sunlight; this agrees with the conclusion that plants need sunlight for growth.
s: Verdict: agrees
A and C get the same water and differ only in sunlight
Concludes the difference is due to sunlight, so sunlight is needed

questions.q:
A school in Ranchi grows marigold seedlings in three trays for ten days. Tray 1 stands in the sun and is watered daily. Tray 2 is watered daily but kept under a cardboard box. Tray 3 stands in the sun and is watered only on the first day. The average heights are: tray 1, 18 cm; tray 2, 11 cm; tray 3, 6 cm (and its leaves have turned yellow).
(a) Match each tray to pot A, B or C of Activity 10.1.
(b) How many centimetres taller is tray 1 than tray 2, and than tray 3? Which missing factor lowered the height more in this data?
(c) Does tray 3's yellowing agree with what the book says about pot B?
(d) The school can fix only one problem this week. Using your answers, which should it fix first?
questions.a: (a) Tray 1 is pot A, tray 2 is pot C and tray 3 is pot B. (b) 7 cm taller than tray 2 and 12 cm taller than tray 3; lack of water lowered the height more. (c) Yes. The book says the plant in pot B may die for want of water, so yellow, stunted growth fits. (d) Water first, because the no-water tray did worse (6 cm against 11 cm), but both sunlight and water are needed in the long run.
s: Part (a): trays matched to pots A, C and B
Part (b): correct differences 7 cm and 12 cm and water named
Part (c): links tray 3 to pot B
Part (d): fixes water first using the data and notes both are needed

questions.q:
A teacher reads the class the Vrikshayurveda lines in the chapter. A student says: 'That book gives manure recipes, but no one ran a three-pot experiment on them, so its ideas have no basis.'
(a) On what does the book say the knowledge in that text seems to be based?
(b) How is this different from the way Activity 10.1 finds out about growth?
questions.a: (a) On practical experiences and patterns seen over time, which were then documented systematically. (b) Activity 10.1 sets up pots deliberately, changes one condition at a time and records heights and leaves in a table over two weeks, while the text records patterns that were observed over time in practice.
s: Part (a): practical experience and patterns seen over time
Part (b): the activity changes one condition under control and records it, the text collects observed patterns

questions.q: Plan a two-pot set-up that tests only the role of sunlight in the growth of a marigold sapling. Say what is kept the same and what is changed.
questions.a: Two pots with same-size saplings and same soil, both watered equally every day. One is kept in direct sunlight and the other in the dark. Observe height and leaves for two weeks.
s: Keeps pots, saplings, soil and water the same
Changes only sunlight: one in sunlight, one in the dark
Says what to observe over two weeks

questions.q: Which statement about plant growth is FALSE?
questions.a: Pot B (sunlight, no water) may die, and pot C (water, no sunlight) grows less, so 'sunlight alone is enough' is false.
o: Sunlight alone is enough for a plant to grow, so watering is optional
A sapling in the dark with water grows less than one in sunlight with water
A sunlit sapling that is never watered may die
Plants need both sunlight and water for their growth

questions.q: A tomato sapling in a pot like pot A is 16 cm tall on Day 1 and 29 cm tall after two weeks, so its mean growth is ___ cm per week.

A school gardener has two corners for tomato saplings: a sunny corner far from any tap, where water must be carried in cans, and a shaded corner next to a tap. Using what you know from Activity 10.1, say what each corner offers, what is likely to happen in each if nothing else is done, and recommend a plan.
questions.a: The sunny corner gives sunlight but water must be carried; if not watered the plants are like pot B and may die. The shaded corner has water but no sunlight; plants are like pot C and grow less. Plants need both, so the gardener should use the sunny corner and arrange regular watering with cans, since sunlight cannot be added to the shaded corner by watering.
s: Sunny corner: sunlight but water is a problem, like pot B
Shaded corner: water but no sunlight, like pot C
Likely result in each corner
Recommends the sunny corner with regular watering
Reason: both sunlight and water are needed and water cannot replace sunlight

questions.q: Two chilli saplings are compared for two weeks. One stands on a sunny terrace and is watered daily. The other is in a windowless store room and is watered three times a day. What does the result most likely support?
questions.a: Pot C (water, no sunlight) grows less than pot A. Extra water is not a substitute for sunlight.
o: The store-room plant grows less, so extra water cannot replace sunlight
The store-room plant grows more, because more water gives more growth
Both plants grow equally, because both are watered every day
The terrace plant grows less, because plants should not get sunlight daily

questions.q:
After two weeks the pot A sapling has grown from 14 cm to 27 cm and the pot C sapling from 14 cm to 19 cm.
(a) How much more did the pot A sapling grow than the pot C sapling?
(b) Name the one condition that explains this difference, and say why the other conditions cannot.
questions.a: (a) A grew 13 cm and C grew 5 cm, so A grew 8 cm more. (b) Sunlight. Both pots get water every day and the soil and sapling size are the same, so only sunlight differs between them.
s: Part (a): 13 cm and 5 cm, so 8 cm more
Part (b): sunlight, because A and C differ only in sunlight

questions.q:
Statement 1: As a plant grows, its height increases and its stem thickens.
Statement 2: A sapling kept in the dark with plenty of water grows as well as a sunlit one.
Statement 3: Two pots that differ only in water let us judge the effect of water on growth.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 is false: pot C, in the dark with water, grows less than pot A.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A student sets up only pots A and B of Activity 10.1 and says she can now tell whether sunlight is needed for growth. Show that she cannot.
questions.a: Pots A and B are both in sunlight; they differ only in water. Nothing in the set-up has a plant without sunlight, so the effect of sunlight cannot be judged. A pot in the dark with water (pot C) is needed.
s: Notes that A and B are both in sunlight
States that they differ only in water
Says a pot kept in the dark with water (pot C) is needed

questions.q: True or False: Sapling P stands 28 cm tall on Day 1 and 30 cm after two weeks. Sapling Q stands 12 cm tall on Day 1 and 22 cm after two weeks. Because P is taller after two weeks, P grew more than Q. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. P grew 30 - 28 = 2 cm and Q grew 22 - 12 = 10 cm. Growth is the change from the Day 1 reading, so the final height alone does not show which plant grew more.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: growth is the change from Day 1; P grew 2 cm, Q grew 10 cm

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The plant in pot C grows less than the plant in pot A.
Reason (R): Pot C is given water every day.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion. Pot C gets water just like pot A; it grows less because it gets no sunlight.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q: Before Activity 10.1 three friends gave explanations for plant growth: Asha said 'regular watering helps plants grow better', Sana said 'sunlight plays some role' and Rohit said 'plants take up food from the soil through their roots'. Using the set-up of pots A, B and C, say what the activity shows about each explanation, and what the activity would have to change to test Rohit's idea.
questions.a: Asha: pot A (watered) grows better than pot B (not watered, may die), so supported. Sana: pot A (sunlight) grows better than pot C (dark), so supported. Rohit: all three pots hold the same garden soil, so the activity does not test his idea, and soil cannot explain the differences seen. To test it, the soil would have to be the condition that differs, with sunlight and water kept the same.
s: Asha's explanation supported by pots A and B
Sana's explanation supported by pots A and C
Rohit's idea not tested: all pots have the same soil
Soil would have to be the one condition changed
Others (sunlight and water) kept the same in that test

questions.q:
Match each record or comparison from Activity 10.1 with what it tells you.
Match Column I with Column II.
1. The Day 1 height of each plant
2. Leaves recorded as yellow in pot B
3. Comparing pot A with pot C
4. Comparing pot A with pot B

a. Isolates the effect of sunlight
b. Isolates the effect of water
c. Gives the starting point from which growth is judged
d. Shows the plant may be in trouble
questions.a: Day 1 height is the starting point; yellow leaves signal trouble; A and C differ only in sunlight; A and B differ only in water.

questions.q: Ritu keeps pot C's sapling in a dark cupboard in a cooler room, while pot A's sapling stands on a sunny window sill. Both are watered daily. After two weeks the cupboard sapling is shorter. What may she conclude?
questions.a: The two pots differ in sunlight and also in temperature, so the shorter growth cannot be put down to sunlight alone.
o: Sunlight alone cannot be blamed, since two conditions differ
Sunlight is proved essential, as one pot is kept in the dark cupboard
Water is shown to be the cause, as both of the pots are watered
The test is invalid, as a cupboard sapling cannot be watered at all

questions.q: The chapter quotes an ancient line: 'Trees do not produce fruits and flowers merely because they are planted.' A village group plants twenty mango saplings in a shaded gully and never waters them. Which reading fits both the line and Activity 10.1?
questions.a: Planting alone is not enough: the saplings also need sunlight and water, as pots B and C suggest.
o: Planting alone is not enough; the saplings also need sunlight and water
Planting is enough, because the line says trees give fruit once the sapling is in the soil
Only water matters, because pot A grew best and was the only pot that was watered
Only sunlight matters, because pot B received sunlight and still grew as well as pot A

questions.q: Sunita believes plants get all their food from the soil. She keeps one sapling in a pot of garden soil in the dark and waters it daily, and keeps a similar sapling in the same kind of soil in sunlight, watered daily. After two weeks the dark one has grown less. What does this suggest about her belief?
questions.a: Both pots have the same soil, yet the dark one grows less, so soil alone does not decide growth; sunlight matters too.
o: Soil alone does not decide growth, since the dark pot has soil and grows less
Her belief is proved, since both pots hold soil and both plants stay alive
Her belief is proved, since the sunlit plant also takes up food from the soil
Roots take up nothing from the soil, since the dark plant grows less than the sunlit one

questions.q:
A student records pot B after two weeks as follows: height 15 cm (Day 1: 14 cm), leaves 4 (Day 1: 9), colour of leaves yellow (Day 1: green).
(a) Why would the height reading alone make pot B look healthier than it is?
(b) Which two columns of Table 10.1 reveal the trouble?
questions.a: (a) The height rose by 1 cm, so the plant seems to have grown a little, although it lost leaves and turned yellow. (b) The number of leaves (9 fell to 4) and the colour of leaves (green turned yellow).
s: Part (a): height rose slightly and hides the damage
Part (b): number of leaves and colour of leaves

questions.q: Bhaskar puts a potted plant in the dark at 6 pm on Monday and keeps it there for 36 hours before picking its leaf, so the leaf is picked at ___ am on Wednesday.
Mira tests a leaf from a sunlit plant only. Its green patches turn blue-black and she writes: 'This proves sunlight is needed to make starch.' Show that her single result cannot prove this.
questions.a: Her result shows only that starch is present in the green patches of a leaf from a plant that was in sunlight. To say sunlight is needed she must compare it with a leaf from a similar plant kept in the dark. In Bhaskar's table that leaf shows no blue-black, even on green patches; without that comparison the starch could have been made in light or in the dark.
s: Notes that her test has sunlight only, with nothing to compare against
Says a similar plant kept in the dark is needed for the comparison
Says Bhaskar's dark-kept leaf (no blue-black) is what actually shows sunlight is needed

questions.q: Justify the statement 'Leaves are the food factories of plants' using the starch test and the test on green and non-green patches.
questions.a: The starch test shows the leaf contains starch, the stored food. In the patch test only the green patches of the sunlit plant's leaf turned blue-black and the dark-kept plant's leaf did not, so starch is made where chlorophyll is present and sunlight is available. Leaves are broad and flat and mostly green, so they capture sunlight efficiently. Hence the food is made in leaves.
s: Starch is found in leaves
Green patches of the sunlit leaf turn blue-black
Dark-kept leaf shows no starch, so sunlight is essential
Chlorophyll is needed, linking to green patches
Broad flat shape and green colour suit capturing sunlight

questions.q:
In a school lab in Kolkata, Ravi decolourises two leaves from a plant that has stood in bright sunlight: a green leaf and a red amaranthus leaf. Both turn blue-black after iodine is added. Ravi writes in his notebook: 'Red leaves have no chlorophyll, and they make starch without it. A red leaf needs no sunlight either.'
(a) What does the blue-black colour in the red leaf tell you?
(b) Is the first sentence of Ravi's note correct? Use what the chapter says about red, violet and brown leaves.
(c) Do his two leaves support his second sentence, 'A red leaf needs no sunlight either'?
(d) To settle it he can use (i) a second red leaf from the same sunlit plant, or (ii) a red leaf from a similar plant kept in the dark for 36 hours, which makes him wait a day and a half. Which should he choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) Starch was made, so photosynthesis took place in the red leaf. (b) Not correct: red leaves contain more of other coloured pigments than chlorophyll, which hides the green; some of these pigments also help in photosynthesis. (c) No. Both of his leaves came from a sunlit plant, so nothing shows what happens without sunlight. (d) Choose (ii): only a leaf kept without sunlight gives a comparison. A second sunlit leaf would give the same result and teach nothing new, so the wait is worth it.
s: Part (a): starch made, photosynthesis took place
Part (b): rejects the sentence using the pigment fact
Part (c): no, both leaves were in sunlight, so there is no comparison
Part (d): chooses the dark-kept red leaf and justifies the wait

questions.q: Neha wants to hurry up decolourising a leaf, so she holds the test tube of alcohol with the leaf in it directly over the flame of a spirit lamp. What does the chapter's activity say is wrong with this?
questions.a: Alcohol is highly flammable, so it should never be put near a direct heat source; the test tube should stand in a beaker of boiling water.
o: Alcohol is flammable, so it is warmed only in a beaker of boiling water
The leaf must be boiled in iodine, not in alcohol, to turn it colourless
Alcohol burns off the starch, so the iodine then shows no change in colour
Nothing is wrong, since the leaf has already been softened by boiling

questions.q: Which statement about leaves is FALSE?
questions.a: Red, violet or brown leaves have other pigments hiding the green, and some of these pigments also help photosynthesis, so 'can never' is false.
o: A leaf that is not green can never help in making food
Leaves are generally broad and flat in their design
Leaves are mostly green because of the pigment chlorophyll
Leaves are called the food factories of the plants

questions.q: A tulsi plant and a coleus plant with red leaves both stand in sunlight. Plan how you will find out whether each of their leaves has made starch. Write the steps in order, the safety precaution and how you will read the result for each plant.
questions.a: Boil one leaf of each plant in water for five minutes to soften it. Put each in alcohol in a test tube kept in a beaker of boiling water until colourless; never heat alcohol directly. Place each leaf on a plate, add diluted iodine and wait. Blue-black means starch is present, for the tulsi leaf and for the red leaf; the red leaf is tested the same way because other pigments only hide its green.
s: Softening both leaves by boiling in water
Decolourising in alcohol in a beaker of boiling water
Safety: alcohol never heated directly
Adding diluted iodine to each leaf
Reading blue-black as starch for each leaf

questions.q:
Before testing the leaves in Activity 10.3, Bhaskar made a sketch on tracing paper to record where the green and the non-green patches lie on each leaf.
(a) Why could he not have noted the patches after the alcohol step instead?
(b) What could he then not have checked about the blue-black colour?
questions.a: (a) Alcohol makes the leaf colourless, so the green and non-green patches can no longer be told apart. (b) He could not have checked whether the blue-black appeared only on the places that were green, so he could not link starch to chlorophyll.
s: Part (a): decolourising removes the colour, so the patches are lost
Part (b): could not link the blue-black areas to the green patches

questions.q: Rohan keeps a variegated money-plant leaf, with green and white patches, in a sunny window for a few days. He decolourises it and adds iodine. What is the most likely result?
questions.a: Starch forms where chlorophyll and sunlight are available; non-green patches may not have enough chlorophyll to make detectable starch.
o: The green patches turn blue-black more than the white patches
Only the white patches turn blue-black, as they have no chlorophyll
The whole leaf turns equally blue-black, as sunlight reaches all of it
No patch turns blue-black, as only dark-kept leaves hold starch

questions.q: Write a set-up with two leaves from similar plants in which one leaf turns blue-black with iodine and the other does not, changing only one condition. Say which leaf turns blue-black and which condition explains the difference.
questions.a: Example: a leaf from a plant kept in sunlight and a leaf from a similar plant kept in the dark for 36 hours, both decolourised and tested with iodine. The sunlit leaf turns blue-black and the dark-kept leaf does not. The condition changed is sunlight, which is needed to make starch. (A single condition of this chapter, such as sunlight, is accepted.)
s: Set-up with two similar plants and only one condition changed
States which leaf turns blue-black
Names the changed condition as the explanation

questions.q:
A student says: 'Iodine turns blue-black wherever a leaf is green.'
(a) Which observation in Table 10.2 contradicts this?
(b) What does iodine actually show with the blue-black colour?
questions.a: (a) The leaf of the plant kept in the dark has green patches but shows no blue-black colour. (b) The blue-black colour shows that starch is present.
s: Part (a): green patches of the dark-kept leaf are not blue-black
Part (b): blue-black shows starch

questions.q: True or False: In the starch test, putting the leaf in alcohol removes the starch from it, so that the iodine can then show the colour more clearly. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The alcohol only makes the leaf colourless (decolourises it) so that the colour change is easy to see; the starch stays in the leaf and is what turns blue-black with iodine.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: alcohol removes the leaf's colour, not the starch

questions.q: Tanya says: 'The green patch of a sunlit leaf turned blue-black because it had chlorophyll and light. The non-green patch did not turn blue-black, so it has no chlorophyll at all.' Agree or disagree with each part.
questions.a: She is right in the first part: starch is made where chlorophyll captures sunlight. The second part goes too far: the non-green patch may not have sufficient chlorophyll to prepare starch that can be detected, which is not the same as having none.
s: First part: agrees, chlorophyll and sunlight make starch
Second part: disagrees, it may only lack sufficient chlorophyll
Reason: test detects only enough starch

questions.q:
The chapter says leaves are by design generally broad and flat, and that chlorophyll helps in capturing sunlight efficiently.
(a) Suggest one way a broad flat surface could help a leaf do its job.
(b) What would you expect for the starch made by a leaf that has little chlorophyll?
questions.a: (a) A broad flat surface presents more area to the sunlight, so more sunlight can be captured for making food (this is reasoning, not a statement made in the book). (b) Less sunlight would be captured, so less starch would be made.
s: Part (a): more surface area to capture sunlight
Part (b): little chlorophyll means less capture and less starch

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Only the green patches of the leaf from the sunlit plant turned blue-black with iodine.
Reason (R): Chlorophyll helps in capturing sunlight efficiently.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion: starch is made where chlorophyll captures sunlight.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q:
A leaf from a sunlit plant is decolourised and tested with iodine. No part of it shows the blue-black colour.
(a) What does this result show?
(b) Does it prove that the plant cannot make starch? Give a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) No starch was detected in that leaf. (b) No. The leaf may have come from a plant kept in the dark, or the part tested may not have sufficient chlorophyll to prepare enough starch to be detected; the test shows only starch that is present in enough quantity.
s: Part (a): no starch was detected
Part (b): not proof; no sunlight or too little chlorophyll for detectable starch

questions.q:
In Fig. 10.2 a leaf lies in alcohol in a test tube, the test tube stands in a beaker of water, and the spirit lamp heats the beaker.
(a) Which liquid is heated directly by the flame?
(b) Why is this arrangement used for the leaf in alcohol?
questions.a: (a) The water in the beaker. (b) Alcohol is highly flammable and must not be put near a direct heat source, so it is warmed only indirectly by the boiling water around its test tube.
s: Part (a): water in the beaker
Part (b): alcohol is flammable, heated indirectly

questions.q: Meera has three leaves from plants that stood in bright sunlight: a leaf that is deep green, a leaf whose green is hidden by a red pigment, and a leaf from a plant kept for 36 hours in the dark. She decolourises each and adds iodine. Which result matches the chapter?
questions.a: The sunlit green leaf and the sunlit red leaf can both turn blue-black; the dark-kept leaf does not.
o: The sunlit green and red leaves can turn blue-black, the dark-kept leaf cannot
Only the sunlit green leaf turns blue-black, because a red leaf cannot make food at all
All three leaves turn blue-black, because every green leaf stores starch in any light
The dark-kept leaf turns blue-black most, because it has had longer to store starch

questions.q:
Statement 1: Leaves of colours other than green, such as red, violet or brown, take no part in photosynthesis.
Statement 2: A blue-black colour on a decolourised leaf shows that starch is present.
Statement 3: Starch is produced in the leaves of a plant, which are by design generally broad and flat.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 is false: some of the other pigments also help in photosynthesis.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
A science teacher in Guwahati tests three leaves from similar plants. Leaf L1 is from a plant kept in sunlight for two days. Leaf L2 is from a plant kept in the dark for 36 hours. Leaf L3 is from a sunlit plant, but a strip of black paper was clipped over its middle during the day. After decolourising, L1 turns blue-black all over, L2 shows no blue-black, and L3 turns blue-black except under the paper strip.
(a) Which two results together show that sunlight is needed for starch?
(b) Why does one leaf, L3, show starch in one part and not in another although it has chlorophyll throughout?
(c) The teacher can test one more leaf: a variegated leaf (green and white patches) from a sunlit plant, or a red leaf from a sunlit plant. Which one tells you more about the role of chlorophyll?
(d) Justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) L2 (no starch in the dark) and L1 (starch in sunlight); L3 also supports it. (b) The covered strip got no sunlight, so no starch was made there, while the rest of the leaf got sunlight. (c) The variegated leaf. (d) On the variegated leaf green and non-green patches share the same sunlight, so the comparison shows the effect of chlorophyll alone; the red leaf has other pigments and does not isolate chlorophyll.
s: Part (a): L1 and L2, with L3 as support
Part (b): the covered strip received no sunlight
Part (c): picks the variegated leaf
Part (d): justifies with the same-sunlight comparison of patches

questions.q:
Match each observation from the starch tests with what it supports.
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Green patches of a sunlit leaf turn blue-black
2. No blue-black anywhere on a leaf from a plant kept in the dark
3. A non-green patch of a sunlit leaf stays unchanged
4. A red leaf from a sunlit plant turns blue-black

a. Sunlight is needed for starch
b. Chlorophyll is linked with starch-making
c. The patch may lack enough chlorophyll for detectable starch
d. Other pigments hide the green, yet photosynthesis happened
questions.a: Green patch + starch links chlorophyll to starch; no starch in the dark shows sunlight is needed; a pale patch may lack enough chlorophyll; a red leaf has other pigments but still makes starch.

questions.q: Justify the statement 'Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen, and it needs sunlight' using one result from Activity 10.4, one from Activity 10.5, and the dark set-up of Activity 10.5.
questions.a: Activity 10.4: the half of the destarched leaf outside the bottle turns blue-black, but the half inside, where caustic soda absorbs carbon dioxide, does not, so carbon dioxide is needed for making starch. Activity 10.5: bubbles collect in the inverted test tube over the sunlit water plant, and a lit matchstick burns with an intense flame in the gas, so the gas is rich in oxygen and oxygen is released. The dark set-up is kept as a comparison: with all else the same it gives no bubbles, so photosynthesis, and the release of oxygen, occurs in the presence of sunlight.
s: Activity 10.4: inside half without carbon dioxide shows no starch
So carbon dioxide is needed for making starch
Activity 10.5: bubbles and the intense matchstick flame show oxygen is released
Dark set-up is the comparison and gives no bubbles
Concludes sunlight is needed for photosynthesis and oxygen release

questions.q: Plan an experiment with the water plant, funnel and inverted test tube to find out whether more light gives more oxygen bubbles. State what you change, what you keep the same, what you observe and how you decide.
questions.a: Make identical set-ups with the same kind and size of water plant. Keep one in bright sunlight and another in a shaded place, changing only the amount of light. Keep water and time the same. Count the bubbles that collect in the same time. If the brighter set-up collects more bubbles, more light gives more oxygen.
s: Identical set-ups of the water plant
Changes only the amount of light
Keeps water and time the same
Counts bubbles collected
States how the comparison gives the decision

questions.q: Four similar, well-watered potted plants are placed as follows: P in sunlight with air around it; Q in sunlight with caustic soda absorbing the carbon dioxide around it; R in the dark with air around it; S in the dark with caustic soda around it. Which plant(s) will form starch and release oxygen?
questions.a: Only P has both sunlight and carbon dioxide.
o: Only P, which has both sunlight and carbon dioxide
P and Q, because sunlight alone is enough for it
P and R, because carbon dioxide alone is enough for it
All four, because every green plant has chlorophyll

questions.q:
Match each observation or step from Activities 10.4 and 10.5 with what it lets you conclude.
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Inside half of the leaf stays unchanged while the outside half turns blue-black
2. A lit matchstick burns with an intense flame in the gas from the sunlit water plant
3. No bubbles collect in the set-up kept in the dark
4. The plant is kept in the dark for two to three days before the experiment

a. Carbon dioxide is essential for making starch
b. The gas collected is rich in oxygen
c. Photosynthesis needs sunlight
d. Starch stored earlier is removed, so any starch found is newly made
questions.a: The comparison of the two halves shows carbon dioxide is needed; the matchstick shows oxygen; no bubbles in the dark shows sunlight is needed; the dark period destarches the plant.

questions.q:
Three similar potted plants are kept in the dark for three days and then placed in plastic bags for a few hours. Plant P stands in sunlight with a dish of caustic soda inside its bag. Plant Q stands in sunlight with a dish of plain water inside its bag. Plant R stands in the dark with a dish of plain water inside its bag. A leaf from each is then tested for starch.
(a) Predict the iodine result for the leaf of each plant.
(b) Why do Q and R also have a dish inside the bag?
(c) The lab has alcohol to decolourise only two leaves this period, and the class wants to know whether carbon dioxide is needed. Which two leaves should be tested?
(d) Can the same pair also show that sunlight is needed? If not, which pair would?
questions.a: (a) P: no blue-black. Q: blue-black. R: no blue-black. (b) So that the three set-ups look alike and differ only in the intended condition (caustic soda for P, darkness for R). (c) The leaves of P and Q: they differ only in whether carbon dioxide is absorbed. (d) No, because both are in sunlight. The pair Q and R would show it, since they differ only in sunlight.
s: Part (a): P no, Q yes, R no blue-black
Part (b): keep conditions alike so one condition differs
Part (c): P and Q, differing only in carbon dioxide
Part (d): no; Q and R would test sunlight

questions.q: A teacher destarches a potted plant for the full three days in the dark, starting on Monday morning, so Activity 10.4 can begin on ___ morning.
questions.a: Thursday

questions.q:
Pallavi repeats Activity 10.4 with a plant that stood in the sun until the morning, skipping the two to three days in the dark. After the experiment both halves of her leaf turn blue-black.
(a) Can she conclude that carbon dioxide is not needed to make starch?
(b) What should she have done first?
questions.a: (a) No. The inside half may have kept starch stored earlier, so its colour does not show whether starch was made during the experiment. (b) Keep the potted plant in the dark for two to three days so it loses its stored starch (destarches).
s: Part (a): no, old stored starch can give the colour
Part (b): destarch by keeping the plant in the dark for two to three days

questions.q:
A student fills Table 10.3 for the part of the leaf inside the bottle in Activity 10.4 as: water Yes, sunlight Yes, chlorophyll Yes, carbon dioxide Yes, starch present No.
(a) Which entry is wrong, and what should it be?
(b) With the entry corrected, which factor explains the starch result?
questions.a: (a) The carbon dioxide entry should be No, because the caustic soda absorbs the carbon dioxide inside the bottle. (b) The missing carbon dioxide explains why no starch is present.
s: Part (a): carbon dioxide should be No (absorbed by caustic soda)
Part (b): carbon dioxide is the missing factor behind no starch

questions.q: A report says: 'Bubbles collected in the inverted test tube in the sunlit set-up; a lit matchstick burnt intensely in the gas; the dark set-up gave no bubbles.' Write the aim and the conclusion of the activity.
questions.a: Aim: to find out whether a gas is released during photosynthesis and whether sunlight is needed. Conclusion: oxygen is released during photosynthesis, and photosynthesis occurs in the presence of sunlight.
s: States a suitable aim
Concludes oxygen is released
Concludes sunlight is needed

questions.q:
Every leaf of a potted plant is covered with black paper on a sunny day, but its green stem is left uncovered.
(a) Can the plant make some food in this state?
(b) What must the stem contain for this to happen?
questions.a: (a) Yes, some. Other parts of a plant that have chlorophyll also perform photosynthesis, though the leaf is the primary site. (b) Chlorophyll, which is why the stem is green.
s: Part (a): yes, green parts other than leaves photosynthesise
Part (b): chlorophyll

questions.q:
Statement 1: Only the leaf of a plant can carry out photosynthesis, never any other green part.
Statement 2: In Activity 10.5 the gas collected in the sunlit set-up lets a lit matchstick burn with an intense flame.
Statement 3: In Activity 10.5 bubbles collect in the dark set-up as well as in the sunlit one.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are false: other parts with chlorophyll also photosynthesise, and the dark set-up gives no bubbles.
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: True or False: In Activity 10.4 the half of the leaf outside the bottle is a useful comparison for the half inside, because the two halves are on the same leaf and differ in their access to carbon dioxide. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Both halves belong to one destarched leaf and get the same sunlight, water and chlorophyll; only carbon dioxide differs, so the different starch results can be put down to carbon dioxide.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: same leaf and conditions, only carbon dioxide differs

questions.q:
Two students suggest changes to Activity 10.4. Meera says: 'Let every student pour the caustic soda to save time.' Ishaan says: 'Put the whole leaf inside the bottle so we need no outside half.'
(a) Evaluate Meera's suggestion.
(b) Evaluate Ishaan's suggestion.
questions.a: (a) Not acceptable: caustic soda is a strong chemical that can cause skin burns, so only teachers should handle it. (b) Not acceptable: with the whole leaf in the bottle no part would get carbon dioxide, so there would be no part making starch to compare with.
s: Part (a): caustic soda causes skin burns, teacher only
Part (b): no outside half means no comparison

questions.q: A water plant with water, chlorophyll and carbon dioxide around it is set up with a funnel and an inverted test tube, and then kept in a dark cupboard. Show that the gas collected in the tube cannot make a lit matchstick burn with an intense flame.
questions.a: In the dark set-up no bubbles are seen, so no gas collects in the tube. Photosynthesis, which releases oxygen, occurs in the presence of sunlight, so with no sunlight no oxygen-rich gas builds up. The matchstick would therefore not show the intense flame seen in the sunlit set-up.
s: States that the dark set-up gives no bubbles
Photosynthesis, and so oxygen release, needs sunlight
So no oxygen-rich gas accumulates for an intense flame

questions.q:
Compare the two pairs of conditions: the two halves of one leaf in Activity 10.4, and set-ups A and B of Activity 10.5.
(a) State the single condition that differs in each pair.
(b) Which of the two activities needs the plant to be destarched first, and why?
questions.a: (a) In Activity 10.4 the halves differ in carbon dioxide (absorbed by caustic soda inside the bottle); in Activity 10.5 the set-ups differ in sunlight (A in sunlight, B in the dark). (b) Activity 10.4, because it tests whether starch is made, and stored starch would confuse the result.
s: Part (a): carbon dioxide for 10.4, sunlight for 10.5
Part (b): 10.4, as it tests for starch and old starch must go

questions.q: Nisha collects the gas from a sunlit water plant in an inverted test tube and pushes in a lit matchstick, which burns with an intense flame. She writes: 'The gas is carbon dioxide, because plants take in carbon dioxide.' Which comment is correct?
questions.a: The intense flame shows the gas is rich in oxygen, which is released in photosynthesis; carbon dioxide is the gas the plant takes in.
o: The flame shows the gas is rich in oxygen, so she mixed up the gas taken in with the gas released
She is right, because an intense flame is how carbon dioxide is detected in the test tube
She is right, because the water plant releases carbon dioxide in the light that falls on it
The test is useless, because a lit matchstick cannot tell one gas from another gas

questions.q:
Anjali puts two identical sprigs of a water plant under funnels, each with an inverted test tube full of water, in two tumblers. Tumbler S stands on a sunny veranda and tumbler T is covered with a thick black cloth. After one hour, tube S has collected gas that made 28 bubbles pass up while tube T has none. She assumes tube S keeps collecting gas at the same rate.
(a) Name the gas in tube S and say how she can check it.
(b) Why does tube T give none?
(c) How many bubbles does she expect in tube S after 3 hours at the same rate?
(d) At the school fair the set-up can run live for only 45 minutes, and the audience will be convinced only if at least 25 bubbles are seen. At the same rate, is 45 minutes enough, and if not, what should she do?
questions.a: (a) Oxygen; a lit matchstick burns intensely in it. (b) Photosynthesis needs sunlight, and the covered plant gets none. (c) 84 bubbles (28 x 3). (d) In 45 minutes she gets 28 x 0.75 = 21 bubbles, less than 25, so it is not enough. She needs at least about 54 minutes (25 / 28 of an hour), so she should start the set-up in the sun about an hour before the audience arrives.
s: Part (a): oxygen, checked with a lit matchstick
Part (b): no sunlight, so no photosynthesis
Part (c): 84 bubbles
Part (d): 21 bubbles in 45 minutes is not enough, so start about an hour earlier

questions.q: A student looks at the water plants in the school aquarium. At 6 am she sees no bubbles on the plants; at noon, with sunlight on the tank, she sees many. Which explanation fits this chapter?
questions.a: Bubbles of oxygen are released during photosynthesis, which occurs in the presence of sunlight.
o: Photosynthesis, which releases oxygen, goes on in sunlight
The plants release oxygen only in the dark, so noon bubbles are odd
The plants release carbon dioxide in sunlight, which bubbles up
Chlorophyll is made only at noon, so bubbles form then

questions.q: Taken together, Activity 10.4 and Activity 10.5 do NOT show which of these?
questions.a: Neither activity tests for oxygen being needed to make starch.
o: Plants need oxygen from the air to make starch
Carbon dioxide is essential for making starch in a leaf
Oxygen is released by a sunlit water plant in bubbles
Sunlight is needed for the release of oxygen gas

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The gas collected over a sunlit water plant makes a lit matchstick go out.
Reason (R): Oxygen is released during photosynthesis.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: The assertion is false: the matchstick produced an intense flame in the gas. The reason is true.
o: The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.

questions.q: Dev says: 'In Activity 10.4 only the half of the leaf inside the bottle teaches us anything, so the half outside the bottle is not needed.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: No. The half outside the bottle has sunlight, water, chlorophyll and carbon dioxide and turns blue-black, so it shows that starch is made when carbon dioxide is available. The inside half, where caustic soda absorbs carbon dioxide, stays unchanged. Only by comparing both halves can we conclude that carbon dioxide is essential.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Outside half turns blue-black, so starch is made when carbon dioxide is present
Comparison with the inside half shows carbon dioxide is essential

questions.q: A potted plant has healthy green leaves, moist soil and ordinary air around it, but it stands in a dark room for a whole day. Reading the word equation of photosynthesis, what do you expect?
questions.a: Carbon dioxide and water are present, but without sunlight the process does not go on, so no glucose or oxygen is made.
o: No glucose is made, since sunlight is needed though carbon dioxide and water are present
Glucose is made more slowly, since carbon dioxide and water alone are enough to make it
Oxygen is released but no glucose is made, since chlorophyll alone does that in the dark
Starch turns back into carbon dioxide and water, since the leaf is in the dark all day

questions.q: Comparing the word equations of photosynthesis and respiration, the gas that is a product of the first and a starting material of the second is ___.
questions.a: oxygen

questions.q: A student writes: 'In photosynthesis a leaf takes in oxygen and water, and gives out carbon dioxide and glucose.' Find the errors, write the correct word equation, and say through which parts of the plant the two raw materials enter and what becomes of the glucose.
questions.a: The two gases are swapped. The leaf takes in carbon dioxide (not oxygen) and gives out oxygen (not carbon dioxide). Correct equation: carbon dioxide + water gives glucose + oxygen, in sunlight with chlorophyll. Carbon dioxide enters from the air through the stomata and water is taken up by the roots. Glucose serves as an instant source of energy, and what is not used at once is converted into starch for storage.
s: Spots that the gases are swapped
Correct word equation with sunlight and chlorophyll
Carbon dioxide enters through stomata
Water taken up by the roots
Glucose gives instant energy and extra is converted into starch

questions.q:
The iodine test on a sunlit leaf turns it blue-black, yet the book says the food actually produced in photosynthesis is glucose.
(a) Which substance does the iodine test detect?
(b) How can the test still show that photosynthesis has taken place?
questions.a: (a) Starch. (b) The glucose made in photosynthesis is converted into starch for storage, so finding starch in the leaf shows that glucose, and hence food, was made there.
s: Part (a): starch
Part (b): glucose is converted to starch, so starch signals photosynthesis

questions.q: Here is the word equation of respiration: Glucose + Oxygen gives Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy. Write the word equation of the process in a leaf that runs in the opposite direction, and name the two things it needs that the first process does not mention.
questions.a: Carbon dioxide + Water gives Glucose + Oxygen. It needs sunlight and chlorophyll, which are written with the equation of photosynthesis (and not with the equation of respiration).
s: Equation: carbon dioxide + water gives glucose + oxygen
Names sunlight as a need
Names chlorophyll as a need

questions.q: Sana says: 'Stomata help the plant only in photosynthesis. In respiration no gases need to be exchanged, so stomata play no part.' Do you agree?
questions.a: No. The book says stomata help in the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide during both photosynthesis and respiration. Respiration takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide, so gases are exchanged and the same pores serve both.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Stomata help gas exchange in both photosynthesis and respiration
Respiration takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide

questions.q: Following R. H. Dastur's interest in water, temperature and colour of light, plan an investigation of the effect of temperature on photosynthesis in a water plant using a funnel and inverted test tube. State what you change, what you keep the same, what you observe and how you would conclude.
questions.a: Use identical water plants in funnels and inverted test tubes. Change only the temperature of the water in each set-up, keeping sunlight, amount of water and plant size the same. Observe the bubbles of oxygen collecting in the test tubes in the same time. A set-up with more bubbles shows more photosynthesis, so the temperature that gives most bubbles suits it best.
s: Uses identical plants in the funnel set-up
Changes only temperature
Keeps light, water and plants same
Observes oxygen bubbles in the same time
Draws a conclusion from the comparison

questions.q: Which statement about the food made in a leaf is FALSE?
questions.a: Glucose is produced first and is later converted into starch, so starch does not appear directly from carbon dioxide and water.
o: Starch is produced directly from carbon dioxide and water, with no glucose stage
Glucose is a simple carbohydrate and also an instant source of energy for the plant
Extra glucose later gets converted into starch, which is kept for storage
Glucose is produced in photosynthesis along with oxygen from the same reaction

questions.q: True or False: The word equations of photosynthesis and respiration use the same four substances (carbon dioxide, water, glucose and oxygen), with what is a starting material in one appearing as a product in the other. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water gives glucose + oxygen. Respiration: glucose + oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + energy. The starting materials of one are the products of the other (respiration also releases energy).
s: Verdict: True
Reason: starting materials and products are swapped between the two equations

questions.q:
A nursery owner near Nashik plans to cover the roof of his tomato polyhouse with a coloured sheet to cut the heat. A botanist tells him that the plant scientist R. H. Dastur studied how the amount of water, temperature and the colour of light affect photosynthesis. The sheet takes a week to fit and cannot be returned.
(a) Which two of these three factors could a coloured sheet change?
(b) Describe a small trial using funnels, water plants and inverted test tubes to compare plants under the sheet and in the open.
(c) How would the owner read the result?
(d) The heat may damage the tomatoes during the week of the trial. Should he wait, cover the whole roof now, or cover half the roof now? Use your answers.
questions.a: (a) The colour of the light reaching the plants and the temperature. (b) Identical water plants, one set-up under the sheet and one in the open in the same sunlight, each with a funnel and an inverted test tube; collect the bubbles for the same time. (c) More oxygen bubbles means more photosynthesis, so if the covered set-up gives clearly fewer bubbles the sheet is harming the plants. (d) Cover half the roof now: it limits the heat damage, and the uncovered half is the comparison for the trial, so the owner can judge before fitting the rest. (Waiting or covering all can be argued only if the reason uses the trial.)
s: Part (a): colour of light and temperature
Part (b): identical set-ups, covered against open, same time
Part (c): compare oxygen bubbles
Part (d): reasoned choice that uses the trial, such as half the roof now

questions.q:
A student writes the word equation of photosynthesis as: Carbon dioxide + Water gives Glucose + Oxygen + Chlorophyll.
(a) Which term is wrongly shown as a product?
(b) What is the role of that term in the process?
questions.a: (a) Chlorophyll. (b) It is the green pigment that is needed for the process to occur and that helps in capturing sunlight efficiently; it is a condition written with the equation, not something produced.
s: Part (a): chlorophyll
Part (b): needed pigment that helps capture sunlight, not a product

questions.q:
For Annual Day, Anita's mother in Hyderabad wants to put a shiny coating on the leaves of a money plant. She can coat only the upper surface of each leaf, or both surfaces. In the school lab Anita saw a peel from the lower surface of a leaf under the microscope, stained with a drop of ink.
(a) On which surface of the leaf did the lab activity show the stomata, and what are stomata?
(b) Which two gases pass through stomata in photosynthesis?
(c) Which plan blocks less of what the lab showed, and what does the book not tell us about the upper surface?
(d) Advise Anita: coat the upper surface only for the event, coat both, or coat neither? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The lower surface; stomata are tiny pores that help in the exchange of gases. (b) Carbon dioxide enters and oxygen leaves. (c) Coating only the upper surface, since the stomata were shown on the lower surface; but the book does not say the upper surface has none. (d) Either coat only the upper surface of each leaf, and only for the event, washing it off afterwards, or coat neither surface; both can be justified because the lab showed pores on the lower surface while the book does not say the upper surface has none. Coating both surfaces is the weakest choice, as it would block the pores seen in the lab that exchange gases for photosynthesis and respiration.
s: Part (a): lower surface, stomata as pores for gas exchange
Part (b): carbon dioxide in, oxygen out
Part (c): upper-surface-only blocks less and the caution about the upper surface
Part (d): upper surface only (temporary) or neither, with the stomata reason; both surfaces rejected

questions.q:
Match each item with the gases that move in or out.
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Photosynthesis in a leaf
2. Respiration in a leaf
3. Stomata
4. Chlorophyll

a. Carbon dioxide taken in, oxygen given out
b. Oxygen taken in, carbon dioxide given out
c. Pores through which both gases pass
d. Pigment that helps in capturing sunlight efficiently
questions.a: Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen; respiration does the reverse; stomata let both gases pass; chlorophyll helps capture sunlight.

questions.q: Suppose all the green plants on an island stopped photosynthesising for a year. Using the chapter's opening ideas, which effect would follow?
questions.a: Animals get their food from plants, directly or by eating animals that eat plants, so food would run short for all animals.
o: Animals would lose their food source, since all food chains start with plants
Animals would be unaffected, since they make glucose from carbon dioxide
Only plant-eating animals would be affected, since meat-eaters make their own food
Plants would stop respiring, but food for animals would stay the same

questions.q:
R. H. Dastur was born in 1896 and died in 1961. He was head of the Botany Department at the Royal Institute of Science, Bombay, from 1921 to 1935.
(a) How old was he when he became head of the department?
(b) For how many years did he hold that post?
s: Part (a): 25 years
Part (b): 14 years

questions.q: Wheat leaves in a field get bright sunlight, have plenty of chlorophyll and normal air, but the soil has been dry for weeks and the plants take up very little water. Using the word equation of photosynthesis, what is the most likely effect?
questions.a: Water is the short raw material, so less glucose is made and less oxygen is released.
o: Less glucose is made and less oxygen is released, because water is short
More glucose is made, because the shortage of water leaves more room for carbon dioxide
No change, because sunlight and chlorophyll alone make glucose from air
Less carbon dioxide is released, because the leaves respire instead of photosynthesising

questions.q:
In bright afternoon sunlight a green leaf releases more oxygen through photosynthesis than it uses in respiration.
(a) Which gas leaves the leaf overall, and through which pores?
(b) At midnight, which of the two processes continues in the same leaf, and which gas now enters it?
questions.a: (a) Oxygen, through the stomata. (b) Respiration continues, because photosynthesis needs sunlight, so oxygen now enters the leaf (and carbon dioxide leaves).
s: Part (a): oxygen through stomata
Part (b): only respiration, oxygen enters

questions.q: A student says: 'A plant gets the glucose it needs from the soil through its roots.' Show from the chapter that this cannot be how a leaf gets its food.
questions.a: The roots take up water and minerals from the soil, not glucose. Glucose is produced in the leaves in photosynthesis from carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll. Plants do not eat food as animals do, so the food is made in the plant itself.
s: Roots take up water and minerals, not glucose
Glucose is made in the leaf from carbon dioxide and water
Plants do not eat food like animals

questions.q:
Plant X has every leaf coated on all surfaces so that no stomata stay open. Plant Y is untouched. Both are watered and stand in sunlight for a day, and then a leaf from each is tested for starch.
(a) Which leaf is expected to show less blue-black colour?
(b) Explain with the word equation of photosynthesis.
questions.a: (a) The leaf of plant X. (b) Carbon dioxide, a raw material, enters through the stomata, and blocked stomata keep it out, so less glucose and hence less starch is made.
s: Part (a): plant X shows less blue-black
Part (b): carbon dioxide cannot enter through blocked stomata, so less glucose and starch

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The oxygen released during photosynthesis leaves the leaf into the air.
Reason (R): Stomata are tiny pores on the surface of leaves that help in the exchange of gases.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true; stomata are the pores through which the gases are exchanged, so the reason explains the assertion.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q:
Statement 1: Glucose is a simple carbohydrate that can act as an instant source of energy.
Statement 2: Glucose that is not needed at once gets converted into starch for storage.
Statement 3: Stomata are tiny pores in the roots through which the plant exchanges gases.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 3 is false: stomata are pores on the surface of leaves.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: In Activity 10.7 the red ink rises up the stem at a steady 4 cm per hour, so a 56 cm stem shows red at its top after ___ hours.
Hardeep says: 'The food made in the leaves of a twig reaches its flowers through the same thin tubes that carried the red ink in Activity 10.7.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: No. The red ink moved up with water in the xylem, which carries water and minerals from the roots. The food made in the leaves is carried to all parts of the plant through a different set of tubes, the phloem.
s: Verdict: disagrees
The ink travelled in the xylem, which carries water and minerals
Food travels in a different set of tubes, the phloem

questions.q:
Statement 1: In Activity 10.7 the twig in plain water is the comparison for the twig in red ink water.
Statement 2: The food made in the leaves reaches the other parts of the plant through the xylem.
Statement 3: Water and minerals taken up by the roots are carried only to the leaves, not to the stem or branches.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 are false: food travels in the phloem, and the xylem is present in the stem, branches and leaves.
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: In Activity 10.7 Zoya doubts that the red ink is responsible for the red flowers and says the twig might turn red by itself. Which part of the set-up lets her check this?
questions.a: The twig in plain water stays white, which shows the red colour comes from the ink.
o: The twig in plain water stays white, so the red colour is due to the ink
The twig in tumbler B alone, because only coloured water can show the path of water
The roots of the twig in tumbler A, which take up the ink from the water in it
The leaves of the twig in tumbler B, which turn red before the stem does

questions.q: Which step does NOT match Activity 10.7?
questions.a: The stems are cut obliquely at the base while kept inside the water, not cut straight in open air and left aside.
o: Cutting the stems straight across in open air and leaving them for an hour
Filling one-third of each of the two tumblers with water
Adding a few drops of red ink to one of the two tumblers only
Observing the twigs again on the next day after setting up

questions.q:
In Fig. 10.8 the xylem carries water and minerals from the roots, while the phloem carries food from the leaves to all parts of the plant.
(a) In which direction does material move in the xylem?
(b) Does food move in the phloem only upwards? Give a reason using where food is made and where it may be stored.
questions.a: (a) Upwards, from the roots to the stem, branches and leaves. (b) No. Food is made in the leaves and goes to all parts of the plant, including roots, where it may be stored, so it also moves down.
s: Part (a): upward from the roots
Part (b): no; food goes from leaves to all parts, including roots where it is stored

questions.q:
A potted tomato plant stands in bright sunlight, but its soil has been dry for a week.
(a) Which tubes bring less to the leaves?
(b) Water is used in photosynthesis. What do you expect for the food the leaves send through the phloem, and why?
questions.a: (a) The xylem brings less water (and the minerals dissolved in it). (b) With less water the leaves can make less food by photosynthesis, so less food is sent through the phloem to the other parts.
s: Part (a): xylem brings less water
Part (b): less water means less photosynthesis and less food sent by the phloem

questions.q: True or False: In Activity 10.7, red ink water in the tumbler travels up the twig in the phloem, because the phloem carries whatever the stem takes in. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The red ink travels up in the xylem, the thin tubes that carry water and minerals upward; the phloem carries the food made in the leaves.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the xylem carries water and ink upward; the phloem carries food

questions.q: Follow two materials in a radish plant: a mineral dissolved in soil water, and a molecule of food made in a leaf. For each, say where its journey starts, which tubes carry it, and where it can end up. Then say which journey stops first if all the leaves are removed, and why.
questions.a: The mineral starts in the soil, is taken up by the roots, travels dissolved in water through the xylem and reaches the stem, branches and leaves. The food starts in a leaf, where it is made in photosynthesis, travels through the phloem to all parts of the plant, and may be stored in parts such as the root. If all the leaves are removed, the food journey stops first, because food is made only in the leaves; the mineral journey, which begins in the roots, is not cut off at once.
s: Mineral starts at the roots and travels dissolved in water
Mineral is carried by the xylem to the stem, branches and leaves
Food starts in the leaf and is carried by the phloem to all parts
Food may be stored, for example in the root
Removing the leaves stops the food journey first, because food is made in the leaves

questions.q:
For Activity 10.7 the book suggests twigs of tender plants with white flowers, such as white sadabahar or balsam.
(a) Which part of the twig takes the red ink in first?
(b) Why are white flowers a better choice than red ones for this activity?
questions.a: (a) The cut end of the stem, which stands in the red ink water. (b) A red colour showing up in a white flower is easy to see, whereas in a red flower a change in colour would not be noticed.
s: Part (a): the cut end of the stem
Part (b): white flowers show the red colour clearly

questions.q:
Ravi puts a white balsam twig in tumbler B with red ink water and a similar twig in tumbler A with plain water. Next day the flowers in A are white and those in B are red. He cuts the upper stem of the twig in B, far above the water, and sees red dots with a magnifying glass. His friend says, 'These red dots are the tubes that carry food.'
(a) What does tumbler A add to Ravi's conclusion?
(b) What do red dots in the upper stem show about the ink's route?
(c) Evaluate the friend's statement.
(d) Ravi now wants to show where food is stored. Which parts could he test, with which test from the book, and why can he not use the red ink for this?
questions.a: (a) The twig in plain water stays white, so the red colour comes from the ink. (b) The ink travelled up through thin tubes of the stem to a part that was never in the water. (c) Wrong: these tubes are the xylem, which carries water and minerals; food is carried by the phloem. (d) Seeds or roots, tested for starch with iodine; the ink moves with water in the xylem and does not show the path of food.
s: Part (a): the plain-water twig shows the colour came from the ink
Part (b): the ink moved up the stem through thin tubes
Part (c): the tubes are xylem for water, food is in the phloem
Part (d): seeds or roots with iodine; ink follows water, not food

questions.q:
A farmer in Odisha grows radish, a root vegetable, and also sells the leaves as greens. A trader offers a good price this week for half the leaves of every plant. The soil is dry.
(a) Where is the food of the radish plant made, and by which tubes does it reach the root?
(b) What do you expect for the stored food in the roots if half the leaves are sold?
(c) The soil is dry. Which tubes bring water to the leaves, and which process in the leaves uses it?
(d) Should he sell half the leaves now? Weigh the trade-off using (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) In the leaves, and the phloem carries it to the root. (b) Less food is made, so less is carried to and stored in the roots, which may stay smaller. (c) The xylem; water is used in photosynthesis. (d) Selling half the leaves brings money now but leaves fewer food factories and so smaller roots, and dry soil already limits the water for photosynthesis in the remaining leaves. He should sell only a few leaves, or water the field first and accept smaller radishes if he sells half; either reasoned choice that uses the three answers is accepted.
s: Part (a): leaves; phloem
Part (b): less food, smaller stored food in the roots
Part (c): xylem; photosynthesis
Part (d): weighs money now against smaller roots using (a) to (c)

questions.q:
Two similar white balsam twigs stand in red ink water, 60 cm long each. The red colour reaches the top of the twig in a cool room after 20 hours and in a warm room after 12 hours.
(a) Find the rate of rise of the ink in each room in cm per hour.
(b) What do the two trials suggest about water movement, and what limits the conclusion?
questions.a: (a) Cool room: 60 / 20 = 3 cm per hour. Warm room: 60 / 12 = 5 cm per hour. (b) In these trials water moved up faster in the warm room; with only one twig in each room, this is weak evidence, and a repeat with more twigs would be needed.
s: Part (a): 3 cm per hour and 5 cm per hour
Part (b): faster in warm room, but one twig each limits the conclusion

questions.q:
The leaves of a radish plant make food in sunlight and its root swells with stored food.
(a) Which tubes carry the food to the root, and which tubes carry water the opposite way, from the root to the leaves?
(b) A pest damages the phloem near the base of the stem. What happens to the food reaching the root, and why can the roots' water still reach the leaves?
questions.a: (a) The phloem carries the food from the leaves; the xylem carries water and minerals upward from the root. (b) Less food reaches the root, so it stores less; water can still move up because the xylem is a separate set of tubes.
s: Part (a): phloem carries food, xylem carries water up
Part (b): less food reaches the root; xylem is separate so water still rises

questions.q: Design an experiment with white-flowered twigs and red ink to find out whether water moves up a stem faster in warm or in cold conditions. State what you change, what you keep the same, what you observe and how you decide.
questions.a: Take two twigs of the same plant, cut obliquely under water, and place each in a tumbler with the same amount of red ink water. Keep one tumbler in a warm place and the other in a cold place, changing only the temperature. Keep the plant, ink, amount of water and time the same. After a fixed time, compare how far the red colour has risen in the stem, leaves and flowers. The twig where the red colour has risen higher shows faster water movement.
s: Same plant twigs in tumblers of red ink water
Changes only temperature, warm against cold
Keeps ink, amount of water and time the same
Observes how far the red colour has risen
Decides: higher red colour means faster transport

questions.q: A farmer cuts all the leaves off a sunflower plant soon after it flowers. Weeks later its seeds are small and poorly filled. Which explanation fits the chapter?
questions.a: The food that would fill the seeds is made in the leaves and carried to them by the phloem, so without leaves there is less to carry.
o: The leaves make the food that the phloem carries to the seeds, so less reached them
The seeds fill with food that the xylem brings up from the soil, and the cut damaged the xylem
The seeds make food from air by themselves, and the cut stopped it
The leaves store the food for the seeds, and removing them removed the store

questions.q: All the leaves of a young bean plant are below a point on its stem, and its pods are above that point. A gardener cuts through the phloem at that point, leaving the xylem. Show that the pods cannot receive food from those leaves through the stem.
questions.a: Food is made in the leaves and travels to other parts through the phloem. With the phloem cut between the leaves and pods, the food cannot pass the cut, so the pods cannot get food from those leaves by that route.
s: Food is made in the leaves
Phloem is the route for food to other parts
The cut blocks the route to the pods

questions.q: Write a short account of a situation in which food made in the leaves of a plant reaches its root, and say how you could check that the root stores food.
questions.a: In sunlight the leaves of a radish plant make food by photosynthesis. The food is carried through the phloem to all parts of the plant, including the root, where it is stored. To check, remove a slice of the root and test it for starch with iodine; a blue-black colour shows that food is stored.
s: Food is made in the leaves in sunlight
The phloem carries it to the root
Iodine test on the root shows starch stored

questions.q: After a night in red ink water, Seema cuts a white balsam stem far above the water level and sees red dots inside it under a magnifying glass. What do these dots show?
questions.a: The ink moved up through thin tubes of the stem to a part that was never in the water.
o: The ink travelled up through tubes to a part never in the water
The stem soaked up the ink through its outer skin, as a sponge would
The phloem carried the ink down from the leaves of the twig
The ink was made inside the stem of the twig during the night

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The flowers of a white-flowered twig kept in red ink water turn red.
Reason (R): The roots of a plant take up water and minerals from the soil.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion: the ink enters at the cut end of the stem and rises through the xylem, so the roots' uptake from soil is not what explains the red flowers.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q:
Match each situation from Activity 10.7 and the chapter with the idea it points to.
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Red ink reaching a white flower
2. Food made in a leaf reaching the root
3. Food kept in seeds and roots
4. Tumbler A with plain water

a. Carried by the xylem
b. Carried by the phloem
c. May be stored in parts of the plant
d. Comparison showing the colour came from the ink
questions.a: The ink travels in the xylem; food travels in the phloem; food may be stored in seeds and roots; the plain-water twig is the comparison.

questions.q: Gaurav says: 'If I dissolve a mineral fertiliser in the water of the tumbler instead of red ink, it too would travel up the stem in the same tubes as the ink.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. The book says that, just like red ink, minerals dissolved in water also move up the stem through the xylem. The ink shows the path of water in the xylem, and the dissolved mineral goes with the water along it.
s: Verdict: agrees
Minerals dissolved in water move up through the xylem like the ink
The ink marks the path of water, which the minerals travel with

questions.q: The flask of germinating moong seeds in Activity 10.8 stays in the dark for 24 hours, so the carbon dioxide that appears cannot come from ___.
questions.a: photosynthesis

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The lime water connected to the flask of germinating seeds turns milky after 24 hours in the dark.
Reason (R): Photosynthesis in the seeds releases carbon dioxide into the flask.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: The assertion is true, but the reason is false: photosynthesis needs sunlight and takes in carbon dioxide; the seeds respire and release it.
o: The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q: A potted plant is kept in complete darkness for two days. Which statement about its leaves and roots is correct?
questions.a: Photosynthesis cannot go on without sunlight, but all parts, green or not, still respire: glucose is broken down with oxygen to give energy.
o: Photosynthesis stops without sunlight, but all parts still respire using oxygen
Respiration stops in the dark, but photosynthesis continues in the green leaves
Both processes stop in the dark, because both need sunlight to work at all
Only the roots respire in the dark, because the leaves are green and need light

questions.q: Activity 10.8 is done with germinating seeds kept in the dark for 24 hours. Which of these CANNOT be concluded from it alone?
questions.a: The activity was done only in the dark, so it does not show that seeds respire only in the dark.
o: Seeds respire only in the dark
Respiring seeds release carbon dioxide
Lime water turns milky with extra carbon dioxide
The flask holds more carbon dioxide than normal air

questions.q: True or False: In Activity 10.8 the lime water turns milky because the germinating seeds release oxygen, which reacts with the lime water. Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. The seeds respire and release carbon dioxide; it is the extra carbon dioxide in the flask that turns lime water milky.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: carbon dioxide, released by the respiring seeds, turns lime water milky

questions.q: Neha says: 'Photosynthesis and respiration are the reverse of each other, so a plant needs only one of them.' Evaluate her claim by comparing the two processes.
questions.a: The equations look reversed: photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water and gives glucose and oxygen; respiration uses glucose and oxygen and gives carbon dioxide, water and energy. But they do different jobs and occur in different places. Photosynthesis happens in green parts in sunlight and makes food. Respiration happens in all living parts and releases energy for growth. A plant needs both.
s: Photosynthesis: materials and products
Respiration: materials and products
Where and when each happens
Different jobs: food made versus energy released
Verdict: needs both

questions.q:
In Activity 10.8 one test tube of lime water is joined to the flask with germinating seeds and a second test tube is left unconnected.
(a) Which one turns milky?
(b) What does the clear second tube tell us about the source of the carbon dioxide?
questions.a: (a) The one joined to the flask. (b) The carbon dioxide does not come from the lime water or the air alone; the extra carbon dioxide is produced by the seeds as they respire.
s: Part (a): the connected tube
Part (b): the seeds are the source of extra carbon dioxide

questions.q: Plan a test, using the apparatus of Activity 10.8, to find out whether the roots of a small plant respire. Say what goes in the flask, what you connect it to, what you keep as a comparison, and what result would show that roots respire.
questions.a: Place the roots of a small plant on wet cotton in a conical flask, cork it and join it with tubes to a test tube of lime water, and keep it in the dark for 24 hours. Set up a second flask with wet cotton only, joined to its own lime water, as the comparison. If the lime water joined to the flask with roots turns milky while the comparison stays clear, the roots released carbon dioxide, so they respire.
s: Roots on wet cotton in the flask, joined to lime water, in the dark for 24 hours
Comparison flask with wet cotton only
Milky lime water against clear shows roots respire

questions.q: Photosynthesis and respiration help keep nature in balance. Using the two word equations only, show how the gas produced by each process is the gas that the other process uses, and say what each process does for the plant.
questions.a: Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water gives glucose + oxygen. Respiration: glucose + oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + energy. Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis and is used in respiration. Carbon dioxide is a product of respiration and is used in photosynthesis. Photosynthesis makes the food (glucose), and respiration breaks glucose down to release energy for growth and development. So each process supplies what the other needs, but they do different jobs.
s: Writes the equation of photosynthesis
Writes the equation of respiration
Oxygen is a product of one and used by the other
Carbon dioxide is a product of one and used by the other
Photosynthesis makes food while respiration releases energy for growth

questions.q: Soaked green gram seeds are sealed in a clean jar for a night in a dark cupboard. Compared with fresh air, what is expected inside the jar next morning?
questions.a: Respiring seeds use oxygen and release carbon dioxide, so the jar holds more carbon dioxide and less oxygen.
o: More carbon dioxide and less oxygen
Less carbon dioxide and more oxygen
The same amounts of both, since seeds are not green
More oxygen and more carbon dioxide, since seeds make both

questions.q:
Dinesh says: 'Respiration is how a plant gets its food, just as eating is for us.'
(a) What does respiration do to glucose?
(b) Which process makes the glucose in the first place?
questions.a: (a) It breaks glucose down, using oxygen, to release energy (with carbon dioxide and water), so it uses food rather than making it. (b) Photosynthesis makes the glucose.
s: Part (a): breaks glucose down to release energy, not make food
Part (b): photosynthesis

questions.q:
It is noon on a bright day.
(a) Which of the two processes, photosynthesis and respiration, are going on in a green leaf of a potted plant?
(b) Which are going on in the plant's roots under the soil at the same time?
questions.a: (a) Both: photosynthesis, since the green leaf has chlorophyll and sunlight, and respiration, since all parts of a plant respire. (b) Only respiration, since roots are non-green parts that get no sunlight, although all parts respire.
